title: You are accused of something you did not do
lede: Someone has said, to people who matter, that you did something. It is not true. You find out second-hand, which means it has already travelled, and the version in circulation is more detailed than the truth ever is.

blocks.text: Someone has said, to people who matter, that you did something. It is not true. You find out second-hand, which means it has already travelled, and the version in circulation is more detailed than the truth ever is.

items: Innocence does not defend itself. An accusation is a story with a shape; a denial without a competing story is just noise inside their story.
Your emotional reaction reads as guilt to people who do not know you well. Outrage and shame look identical from the outside, which is deeply unfair and completely true.
The people deciding are rarely weighing evidence. They are weighing which of you seems more likely to be lying, based on tone.
Over-explaining is the single most damaging instinct. Long, detailed, emotional defences make listeners feel they are being managed.

items.detail: One sentence. No adjectives, no "I would never in a million years." Flat, calm, specific: this did not happen.

items.move: Ask for the specific claim in writing
items.detail: Vague accusations survive because they are vague. Forcing specificity — when, where, who saw it — is how false claims begin to collapse.

items.move: Stop talking to everyone except the decider
items.detail: Every extra person you plead with becomes another retelling you do not control. Identify who actually decides and talk to them.
Timestamps, calendar entries, card transactions, message threads, door logs. Mundane records are far more persuasive than character witnesses.

items.move: Offer a process, not an argument
items.detail: Ask for the thing a guilty person would avoid: an investigation, a meeting with both parties, a review of the records.

items.move: Write your own account before it drifts
items.detail: Same day. Your memory will be reshaped by every retelling, and a contemporaneous note is treated as evidence.

items.say: "That did not happen. I want to know exactly what I am supposed to have done, and when, so I can address it properly."
"Can you tell me the date and who else was present? I am not able to respond to something this general."
"I would like this looked into formally rather than settled by rumour. I am happy to hand over anything you need."
"I understand you have to take it seriously. I am asking you to take my answer equally seriously."

items: Confronting the accuser alone and unrecorded. It hands them a second story about your behaviour.
The counter-attack. Attacking their character makes it a feud between two unreliable people, which is exactly the outcome a false accuser wants.
Apologising "for how it came across" to make the tension stop. It will be quoted as an admission.
Sarcasm. It is the tone of guilty people in every room you will ever be judged in.
Deleting anything. Even innocent deletion looks like destruction of evidence.
Get the outcome in writing. Verbal exoneration evaporates when the manager leaves.
Do not demand public humiliation of the accuser, even when you have won. It reopens the story with you as the aggressor.
Notice who backed you and who went quiet. Adjust your expectations of the quiet ones without announcing it.
Accept that a residue will remain with some people. You cannot clean it all; you can outlast it.

limit: If the accusation is criminal, or could cost you your licence, job, or access to your children — stop responding on your own. Say "I want to answer this properly and I am getting advice first," and get a lawyer or union representative before the next conversation.
